label: The Twelve — Part 5 — Zekhariyahu 9–14 and Malakhi
summary_plain: Zekhariyahu declares: YHWH will be a wall of fire around Yerushalayim and the glory within her. Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye. Your king comes to you — righteous and having salvation, humble, riding on a donkey. I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Yerushalayim a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy — they will look on me, the one they have pierced, and mourn for him. On that day a fountain shall be opened for the house of David for sin and uncleanness. YHWH's feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives, and it shall split in two. Living waters shall flow out from Yerushalayim. And YHWH shall be king over all the earth — on that day YHWH shall be one and his name one. Malakhi — the last of the Twelve — declares: I have loved you, says YHWH. A son honors his father — if I am a father, where is my honor? Behold, I send my messenger to prepare the way before me. Behold, I will send you Eliyahu the prophet before the great and awesome Day of YHWH.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Minor Prophets Scroll (4QXII) and the Orit Ge'ez. Zekhariyahu 9-14 (often called Deutero-Zechariah) contains some of the most heavily cited prophetic material in the NT: the king on a donkey (9:9), the thirty pieces of silver (11:12-13), the pierced one (12:10), the smitten shepherd (13:7), the Mount of Olives splitting (14:4). The wall of fire around Yerushalayim (2:5) and 'whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye' (2:8) establish YHWH's direct protective relationship with the city. Zekhariyahu 14:9 — 'YHWH shall be one and his name one' — is the eschatological Shema: the full realization of YHWH's sole sovereignty over all the earth. Malakhi — whose name means 'my messenger' — closes the Twelve with the promise of Eliyahu's return before the Day of YHWH.

key_terms.definition: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Tzion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Yerushalayim! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey.' Ancient source; NT borrowed this.
The shepherd's wages valued at thirty pieces of silver — 'the lordly price at which I was priced by them' — YHWH commands it cast to the potter in the house of YHWH. Ancient source; NT borrowed this.

key_terms.term: Look on the One They Pierced (12:10)
key_terms.definition: YHWH declares: 'I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Yerushalayim a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him.' Ancient source; NT borrowed this.

The last of the Hebrew prophetic books; a series of disputations in which YHWH addresses the community's spiritual negligence, priestly failures, mixed marriages, tithing violations, and final appeals to return.

'Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming.' Ancient source; NT borrowed this.
'Return to me, and I will return to you, says YHWH of Hosts. But you say, How shall we return?' — the community's question and YHWH's invitation paired together.
'But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall.'

YHWH's final prophetic word: 'Behold, I will send you Eliyahu the prophet before the great and awesome day of YHWH comes.' Ancient source; NT borrowed this, applying it to their John the Baptist character.

key_terms.term: YHWH King Over All the Earth (14:9)
key_terms.definition: The climactic declaration of Zekharyah's final vision: 'And YHWH will be king over all the earth. On that day YHWH will be one and his name one.'
'On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Yerushalayim, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness.'

faq.question: What makes Zekharyah 9–14 different from chapters 1–8?
faq.answer: Chapters 1–8 are dated oracles tied to specific years of Daryavesh's reign, structured around the night visions. Chapters 9–14 are undated 'burden' oracles of cosmic scope — covering cosmic warfare, national judgment, the coming king, and final universal transformation. Many scholars see them as later additions; regardless of composition history, they are preserved together as one prophetic book.

faq.question: How many times did NT writers borrow from Zekharyah 9–14?
faq.answer: Extensively. The king on a donkey (9:9) is borrowed for the entry into Yerushalayim narrative. The thirty pieces of silver (11:12-13) is borrowed for the betrayal narrative. The pierced one (12:10) is borrowed for crucifixion imagery. The shepherd struck and flock scattered (13:7) is borrowed for a garden scene narrative. 'Look, he is coming with the clouds' in the NT book of Revelation borrows from 12:10. All of these are ancient Zekharyah texts — the NT is the borrower.

faq.question: What is the significance of Zekharyah 14:9 — 'YHWH will be king over all the earth'?
faq.answer: Zekharyah 14:9 is the theological destination of the entire prophetic corpus: YHWH's universal kingship established over every nation, with no competing claims. The Shema's words — 'YHWH is one' — become the universal confession. This is the covenant community's ultimate hope: not Yisra'el's political dominance but YHWH's undivided sovereignty over all creation.

faq.question: What is the book of Malakhi about and when was it written?
faq.answer: Malakhi means 'my messenger' — possibly a title rather than a personal name. The book addresses the Persian-period community (post-exile, after the Temple was rebuilt) and targets specific abuses: careless priests offering defective sacrifices, men divorcing their covenant wives, failure to tithe, and spiritual fatigue. YHWH engages in direct disputation — stating a charge, then voicing the people's objection, then answering it.

faq.question: What does Malakhi 3:1 say about the messenger, and how was it used by NT writers?
faq.answer: Malakhi 3:1 announces YHWH's messenger who will prepare the way before YHWH comes to the Temple. This is YHWH's own herald. NT writers took this ancient text and applied it to their John the Baptist character as a prefiguration. The original text is about YHWH's direct coming to the Temple; the NT recontextualizes it into a preparatory figure for the invented figure.

faq.question: What is the challenge of Malakhi 3:10 about tithing?
faq.answer: Malakhi 3:10 contains one of the rare places YHWH explicitly invites the community to test the divine promise: bring the full tithe into the storehouse and see if YHWH does not open the windows of heaven with blessing. The community had been withholding tithes, and YHWH names this as robbery — robbing from YHWH directly. The challenge is to full covenant obedience and trust.

faq.question: What does 'Eliyahu before the Day of YHWH' mean in Malakhi 4:5?
faq.answer: YHWH promises to send Eliyahu the prophet before the great and terrible Day of YHWH — a figure who will turn the hearts of parents to children and children to parents, preventing YHWH's coming in destruction. This ancient Hebrew expectation of Eliyahu's return became a source text that NT writers borrowed for their John the Baptist character and later their transfiguration scene. Eliyahu's return is rooted in Malakhi, not the NT.

faq.question: What priestly failures does Malakhi condemn?
faq.answer: Malakhi 1–2 details the priests' contempt for YHWH's altar: offering blind, lame, and sick animals for sacrifice — things they would never offer to a human governor. YHWH says it would be better to shut the Temple doors than continue such empty ritual. The priests also corrupted the Torah's teaching and showed partiality in judgments, violating the covenant YHWH made with Levi.

faq.question: How does Malakhi's 'Sun of Righteousness' image function in Malakhi 4:2?
faq.answer: YHWH promises that for those who fear the divine name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings — like calves released from their stalls leaping with energy. The image contrasts with the Day of YHWH's fire for the arrogant: destruction on one hand, healing and freedom on the other. The same day brings both outcomes depending on one's covenant standing.

faq.question: What does Zekharyah's final vision of the nations coming to Yerushalayim mean?
faq.answer: Zekharyah 14 describes YHWH's final transformation of Yerushalayim: enemies attacking, YHWH intervening, the Mount of Olives splitting, living waters flowing east and west year-round, and the survivors of all nations coming up annually to worship YHWH and keep the Festival of Sukkot. Nations that refuse will receive no rain. YHWH's universal kingship means universal covenant accountability.
